name: Kombucha ferment

lead: Kombucha ferment is made by fermenting tea or botanical extracts with a kombucha culture of bacteria and yeast. It appears in serums and toners, where people use it for fresher, brighter, calmer-looking skin.

The chain is antioxidant: the fermentation converts sugars into organic acids and alters the extract's polyphenols, and lab studies report higher antioxidant activity in some fermented extracts. The idea is less oxidative stress on skin and a healthier-looking complexion. Published work so far consists of laboratory studies on cells and chemical assays; human skincare trials were not found.

paras: Applied as a toner, essence or serum after cleansing, usually in a morning and evening routine alongside a moisturiser and sunscreen. It tends to be one of several botanical steps in a K-beauty-style routine. Users describe the effect as a gradual change in freshness over a few weeks.

Topical safety data were not found. Reports of serious adverse events relate mainly to drinking home-brewed kombucha rather than skincare. As with any new topical, a patch test on a small area is the usual precaution for reactive skin.

angle.text: Kombucha ferment goes into serums and toners as an antioxidant, calming botanical aimed at fresher, brighter-looking skin. Lab studies on fermented extracts report higher antioxidant activity, which is the route to less oxidative stress on the skin surface.

lead: Kombucha ferment is a skincare ingredient name for products made by fermenting tea or plant extracts with a kombucha culture (a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, often called SCOBY).[1] Brands add it to serums, toners and masks with the aim of calmer, brighter, more even-looking skin, on the reasoning that fermentation produces organic acids and modifies polyphenols, giving antioxidant and soothing extracts.[1][2]

Kombucha as a drink is a lightly sweetened fermented black tea, thought to have originated in China.[1] Laboratory work has fermented botanical extracts with kombucha cultures and measured antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, including a 2023 study of elderberry (Sambucus nigra) fruit ferment on human skin fibroblast cells.[2]

Among lifters and gut-health followers, kombucha is more often discussed as a drink; a T Nation poster described it as fruity, low in sugar and rich in polyphenols and probiotics, while others mention it among fermented foods for digestion.[3][4] No human trials of kombucha ferment as a skincare ingredient were found.

paras: Kombucha is usually made from sweetened tea fermented by a culture whose yeasts commonly include Saccharomyces cerevisiae and whose bacteria include Komagataeibacter xylinus. The finished drink contains organic acids, polyphenols and small amounts of alcohol and has a pH around 3.5.[1]
Its popularity spread from China to Russia and Europe, became a health fad in Japan after a 1974 bestseller, and grew in the United States from the late 1990s.[1]

A 2023 study compared elderberry fruit extract with a version fermented using kombucha culture, assessing chemical composition, antioxidant activity, and effects on lipopolysaccharide-stimulated human skin fibroblasts.[2] A 2022 study found antioxidant activity of kombucha-fermented goji (Lycium barbarum) broth was 16.51% higher than the infusion.[5] These are cell-based or chemical assays.

Wikipedia notes there is no clinical proof of the many health benefits claimed for the drink; a 2003 review by Ernst did not recommend it therapeutically and a 2019 review found one human study. Rare serious adverse events, including contamination and liver or kidney effects in home-brewed versions, have been reported.[1] These concern ingestion, not topical ferments.
No studies found on kombucha ferment applied to skin. Related work is limited to in vitro studies of fermented plant extracts.[2][5]
